quiz.title: Decision Trees for Practical Work
quiz.description: Fifty questions on decision-tree workflow, split criteria, implementation choices, common pitfalls, evaluation, and production use.

learningMaterial.title: Decision Trees: From Node Impurity to Reliable Models
learningMaterial.summary: A visual study guide explaining how a tree chooses splits, why tiny leaves overfit, and how pruning supports practical generalization.

sections.title: A prediction follows one path
paragraphs: The root node applies the first condition, internal nodes apply later conditions, and a leaf returns the final class, probability, or regression value.
One prediction only depends on features used along its root-to-leaf path. A leaf is defined by having no outgoing split, not by being drawn on the lowest row.
keyPoints: Depth counts edges on the longest root-to-leaf path

illustration.title: One sample moving through a tree

items.label: Root
items.detail: Age less than or equal to 30?

items.label: Internal node
items.detail: Income less than or equal to 50?

sections.title: Impurity measures class mixture inside a node
paragraphs: A sample normally has one target label. Impurity describes how mixed the labels are across all samples currently inside one node.

For Gini impurity, G(S) = 1 - sum of squared class probabilities. A pure node has Gini 0, while a balanced binary node has the maximum Gini value 0.5. Entropy expresses the same uncertainty idea with logarithms.
keyPoints: Impurity belongs to a group of samples inside a node
Lower impurity means the node is easier to classify
Pure does not automatically mean reliable when the node contains very few samples

illustration.title: Class distributions and binary Gini impurity

sections.title: Choose the largest weighted impurity reduction
paragraphs: For each candidate feature and threshold, split the samples, calculate every child impurity, and weight each child by its sample count.

Gain equals parent impurity minus weighted child impurity. The greedy tree chooses the candidate with the largest gain at the current node. Weighting matters because a tiny pure child should not hide a large impure child.
keyPoints: Generate candidate feature and threshold pairs
Select the highest positive gain and repeat recursively

illustration.title: Two splits from a parent with Gini 0.50

items.label: Candidate A
items.detail: Children 2-0 and 3-5. Weighted Gini 0.375, so gain is 0.125.

items.label: Candidate B - choose
items.detail: Children 4-1 and 1-4. Weighted Gini 0.320, so gain is 0.180.

sections.title: Generate valid candidate splits
paragraphs: For a numeric feature, sort the distinct observed values and test midpoints between adjacent values. Duplicate values do not create additional thresholds.

For nominal categories, arbitrary integer encoding can impose a false order. CART may then test only contiguous groups under that order and miss the best category partition. Use supported categorical handling or a validated encoding pipeline.

items.label: Choose
items.detail: Keep the threshold with maximum gain

sections.title: Control complexity with leaf size and pruning
paragraphs: With min_samples_leaf=5, a candidate split is valid only when both resulting children contain at least five training samples. This prevents rules supported by only one or two unusual records.

Pre-pruning blocks excessive growth during training with limits such as max_depth, min_samples_leaf, and min_impurity_decrease. Post-pruning grows a larger tree and then removes weak subtrees, commonly using cost-complexity pruning controlled by ccp_alpha.
keyPoints: Stronger regularization can reduce overfitting but may cause underfitting
Choose pruning settings with validation or cross-validation

illustration.title: Two times to control tree growth

items.label: Pre-pruning
items.detail: Stop an invalid or weak split before its branch grows.

items.label: Post-pruning
items.detail: Grow candidate branches first, then replace weak subtrees with leaves.

sections.title: A practical modeling workflow
paragraphs: Reliable evaluation begins before the model is trained. Define the prediction moment and metric, protect a final test set, and fit preprocessing only on training data.
Tune tree complexity on validation data, inspect errors and leaf sample counts, evaluate once on the final test set, and monitor input drift and real outcomes after deployment.
keyPoints: Avoid target leakage and repeated decisions based on the test set
Use class-aware metrics for imbalanced targets
Do not treat impurity-based feature importance as proof of causality
Monitor missing values, unseen categories, subgroup behavior, and delayed labels

questions.prompt: What does a supervised-learning model learn from a labeled dataset?

options.text: A mapping from input features X to target y
A list of rules that must be written manually before seeing data
Only the average value of every feature
A way to remove the target column

questions.explanation: Supervised learning uses examples containing both features X and target y to learn a mapping that can predict y for new inputs.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly distinguish classification from regression?

options.text: Classification predicts a discrete category
Regression predicts a continuous value
A decision tree can be used for both tasks
Regression always produces only True or False

questions.explanation: Classification outputs class labels, regression outputs numeric values, and decision-tree variants support both tasks.

questions.prompt: Why is a decision tree often compared with an if-then-else program?

options.text: Each internal condition sends a sample down a branch until a leaf returns an output
It executes every branch for every sample
It can only use Boolean input features
Its rules must always be hand-written

questions.explanation: A tree evaluates conditions sequentially along one path, just like nested if-then-else rules, but training learns the rules from data.

questions.prompt: Which roles are matched correctly to decision-tree node types?

options.text: Root node: the first split applied to the data
Internal node: a later condition that splits incoming samples
Leaf node: a terminal node that returns a prediction
Leaf node: any node that happens to be drawn on the lowest row

questions.explanation: Node type is determined by function, not drawing position. A leaf has no outgoing split even if other branches continue deeper.

questions.prompt: A longest root-to-leaf path contains four nodes. What is the tree depth under the usual edge-counting definition?
questions.explanation: Depth counts edges, not nodes. Four nodes on the longest path are connected by three edges.

questions.prompt: Which input-data types can a decision-tree problem contain?

options.text: Numeric features such as age or humidity
Categorical features such as weather type
A mixture of numeric and categorical features
Only features already scaled to the interval 0 to 1

questions.explanation: Tree concepts support numeric, categorical, and mixed data. Exact preprocessing support depends on the chosen software implementation.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a classification node to be pure?

options.text: All samples in the node have the same class label
All feature values have been normalized
The node contains exactly two samples
The node has equal numbers from every class

questions.explanation: Purity describes label consistency. A node containing only one class has no class uncertainty and needs no further split for classification.

questions.prompt: What does entropy measure inside a classification node?

options.text: Uncertainty or class-label disorder
The physical memory used by the model
The number of input columns only
The distance between feature vectors

questions.explanation: Entropy is the average information or uncertainty of the class distribution in a node.

questions.prompt: For a binary node, when is entropy maximal?

options.text: When the two classes are present in equal proportions
When every sample belongs to one class
When the node has exactly one sample
Whenever the positive class is more common

questions.explanation: A 50/50 binary node is maximally uncertain, giving entropy 1 with base-2 logarithms. Entropy approaches 0 as one class dominates completely.

questions.prompt: Using base-2 logarithms, what is the entropy of a pure classification node? Enter the numeric value.
questions.explanation: A pure node has probability 1 for one class and 0 for the others, so its entropy is zero.

questions.prompt: A binary node contains 75% blue samples and 25% red samples. What is its Gini impurity?
questions.explanation: Gini = 1 - (0.75 squared + 0.25 squared) = 0.375.

questions.prompt: What is the Gini impurity of a binary node with a 50/50 class distribution?
questions.explanation: Gini = 1 - (0.5 squared + 0.5 squared) = 0.5, the maximum for two classes.

questions.prompt: Why must child impurities be weighted by child sample counts when evaluating a split?

options.text: A tiny pure branch should not hide a large impure branch
Weighting guarantees every leaf has the same size
Weighting converts categories into numbers
Weighting always makes the gain equal to one

questions.explanation: The split quality must reflect all samples. A pure branch holding only a few records may be outweighed by a large mixed branch.

questions.prompt: Which expression correctly describes impurity gain for a candidate split?

options.text: Parent impurity minus the sample-weighted average child impurity
Parent impurity plus the unweighted child impurities
The number of children divided by the number of features
Training accuracy minus test accuracy

questions.explanation: Information Gain and Gini Gain quantify how much a split reduces impurity relative to the parent node.

questions.prompt: At a node, candidate features have gains 0.226, 0.015, 0.151, and 0.048. Which should the greedy algorithm choose?

options.text: The feature with gain 0.226
The feature with gain 0.015
The feature with gain closest to zero
A random feature because all gains are positive

questions.explanation: The standard greedy rule selects the candidate with the largest immediate impurity reduction. In the Play Tennis example, this makes Outlook the root.

questions.prompt: Why is ordinary decision-tree training called greedy?

options.text: It chooses the best local split at each node without globally searching every possible tree
It always creates the deepest possible tree
It uses every feature in every prediction
It optimizes only inference speed

questions.explanation: Exhaustively comparing all complete trees is impractical, so common algorithms commit to the best split available at the current node.

questions.prompt: For a numeric feature, which steps correctly generate the usual threshold candidates?

options.text: Sort the distinct observed values
Take midpoints between adjacent distinct values
Evaluate the impurity reduction for each candidate
Create additional thresholds between duplicate copies of the same value

questions.explanation: Only adjacent distinct values create meaningful boundaries. Duplicate copies do not create a new partition.

questions.prompt: The distinct sorted delivery times are 10, 15, 20, and 28 minutes. Which threshold set should be evaluated?

options.text: Only 19

questions.explanation: The candidates are the midpoints of consecutive distinct values: (10+15)/2, (15+20)/2, and (20+28)/2.

questions.prompt: In the delivery-time example, thresholds 12.5, 17.5, and 24 have Gini Gains 0.1000, 0.0556, and 0.2500. Which threshold is selected and why?

options.text: 24, because it has the largest Gini Gain
17.5, because it is the middle threshold
12.5, because smaller thresholds are preferred
All three, because a numeric feature must create three children

questions.explanation: The selected threshold is the one that most reduces weighted impurity, not necessarily the numerical midpoint of the full range.

questions.prompt: What is the key split-structure difference emphasized between CART and ID3?

options.text: CART uses binary splits, while ID3 can use multi-way splits
CART only supports regression, while ID3 only supports clustering
CART cannot split numeric features
ID3 always produces a tree of depth one

questions.explanation: CART recursively creates two children. Classical ID3 can create one branch per categorical value.

questions.prompt: A categorical feature has values Sunny, Overcast, and Rain. Which binary partitions must be considered to fully evaluate a CART-style split?

options.text: Sunny versus {Overcast, Rain}
Overcast versus {Sunny, Rain}
Rain versus {Sunny, Overcast}
Only the alphabetical partition

questions.explanation: For three categories, these are the three unique non-trivial binary groupings. Missing one can hide the best split.

questions.prompt: Why can arbitrary integer encoding of a nominal category change the learned CART tree?

options.text: Numeric thresholding only tests contiguous groups under the imposed integer order
Integer encoding changes the target labels automatically
Trees require every category to have a real physical distance
The row order is always shuffled after encoding

questions.explanation: A nominal category has no natural order, but ordinal integers create one. Threshold splits may then miss a useful non-contiguous grouping.

questions.prompt: Which are reasonable ways to avoid misleading ordinal structure for nominal features?

options.text: Use an implementation with native categorical split support
Use a carefully fitted one-hot encoder when appropriate
Document and validate the effect of any encoding strategy
Assign integers arbitrarily and assume the result is invariant

questions.explanation: Encoding is part of the model. It must preserve the intended meaning and be fitted consistently inside the training pipeline.

questions.prompt: What is target leakage?

options.text: Training with a feature that contains target information unavailable at prediction time
Using a small max_depth
Dropping a feature with many missing values
Saving predictions to a file

questions.explanation: Leakage creates unrealistically strong validation results because the model receives information it would not have in real use.

questions.prompt: Why should preprocessing transformations be fitted using training data only?

options.text: Fitting on validation or test data leaks information and makes evaluation optimistic
Decision trees cannot accept transformed test data
It guarantees 100% test accuracy
It makes all features normally distributed

questions.explanation: Encoders, imputers, feature selection, and similar learned transformations should be fitted within a training-only pipeline.

questions.prompt: What is the safest role of a final test set?

options.text: Estimate generalization once after model and hyperparameter choices are finalized
Repeatedly choose max_depth until test accuracy is highest
Train the final tree before validation
Replace missing training labels

questions.explanation: Repeated test-set decisions overfit the test set. Use training and validation or cross-validation for selection, then test once.

questions.prompt: For an imbalanced fraud-classification problem, which checks are more informative than accuracy alone?

options.text: Precision and recall for the fraud class
A confusion matrix
PR-AUC or another metric suited to rare positives
Only the depth printed by the tree

questions.explanation: A majority-class predictor can have high accuracy while missing nearly all rare positives. Per-class and ranking metrics reveal that failure.

questions.prompt: False negatives are much more expensive than false positives. What should guide model selection?

options.text: A metric or cost function reflecting that business asymmetry
Training accuracy only
The tree with the most leaves
Alphabetical feature order

questions.explanation: The validation objective should represent real error costs. Class weights or decision-threshold choices may also be appropriate.

questions.prompt: A full-depth tree scores 1.00 on 10 training samples but 0.55 on 200 new samples. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Overfitting
Underfitting
Perfect generalization
A regression-only problem

questions.explanation: The large train-to-new-data performance gap suggests that the tree memorized training-specific patterns instead of generalizing.

questions.prompt: Which observations are practical warning signs of an overfit decision tree?

options.text: Very high training performance but much lower validation performance
Deep branches ending in leaves with one or very few samples
Rules that change greatly after a small change to the training data
Training and validation errors are both high and similar

questions.explanation: Tiny leaves and unstable deep rules often capture noise. High and similarly poor train/validation error is more consistent with underfitting.

questions.prompt: How does reducing max_depth usually help an overfit tree?

options.text: It limits the number of sequential rules and reduces model complexity
It adds more candidate features
It forces every leaf to be pure
It changes classification into regression

questions.explanation: A shallower tree has fewer opportunities to create narrow rules for noise, trading some training fit for better generalization.

questions.prompt: What practical behavior does increasing min_samples_leaf encourage?

options.text: Each terminal rule must be supported by more training examples
Every node must use more features
The target is converted to a continuous value
All missing values are deleted

questions.explanation: Requiring larger leaves prevents the model from creating special-case rules supported by only one or two records.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between min_samples_split and min_samples_leaf?

options.text: The first controls whether a node may split; the second controls the minimum samples in each resulting leaf
They are two names for exactly the same setting
The first is for regression only and the second for classification only
The first controls feature count and the second class count

questions.explanation: A node needs enough samples before splitting, and every permitted split must also respect the minimum leaf size.

questions.prompt: What is post-pruning intended to do?

options.text: Remove weak branches from a grown tree to improve the complexity-versus-fit tradeoff
Add every possible threshold after training
Convert all leaves back into root nodes
Guarantee that training accuracy increases

questions.explanation: Cost-complexity pruning, such as tuning ccp_alpha, accepts a small fit loss when it removes branches that may not generalize.

questions.prompt: How should max_depth, min_samples_leaf, or pruning strength normally be chosen?

options.text: Compare candidates with validation data or cross-validation using the task metric
Choose the setting with the highest training accuracy
Always use the library default without checking
Use the test set after every trial

questions.explanation: Hyperparameters should be selected on unseen validation folds with a metric tied to the real objective, while preserving the final test set.

questions.prompt: Why is standard feature scaling usually unnecessary for ordinary decision trees?

options.text: Tree splits depend on ordering and thresholds, not Euclidean distance or gradient magnitude
Trees can only use integer features
Scaling would always remove missing values
Scaling prevents classification

questions.explanation: A monotonic rescaling changes threshold numbers but normally preserves the ordering and possible partitions.

questions.prompt: What should a robust workflow do about missing feature values?

options.text: Measure how much is missing and whether the pattern is informative
Use a model with supported missing-value handling or fit an imputer in the pipeline
Apply the same learned handling at training and inference time
Silently treat every missing value as zero without checking meaning

questions.explanation: Missingness needs an explicit, repeatable policy. Zero may be a real value and is not a universally valid substitute.

questions.prompt: A new categorical value appears in production but was absent during training. What is the key requirement?

options.text: The preprocessing pipeline must define a safe unknown-category behavior
The model should map it to the target label
The request must always be discarded
The category should receive a random integer

questions.explanation: Production inputs evolve. Encoders should handle unknown values deterministically, and monitoring should surface their frequency.

questions.prompt: What value does a standard regression-tree leaf predict?

options.text: The mean target of training samples in that leaf
The nearest feature value
The global maximum target
A class probability only

questions.explanation: With squared-error regression, the leaf value that minimizes error is the mean of the targets reaching that leaf.

questions.prompt: When building a squared-error regression tree, what makes one candidate split better than another?

options.text: It produces a lower sample-weighted child mean squared error
It produces the largest number of classes
It always splits at the mean feature value
It gives both children the same prediction

questions.explanation: Regression splits seek child groups whose targets vary less around their respective leaf means.

questions.prompt: In the course salary example, predictions for 5.3 years at max_depth 1, max_depth 2, and unlimited depth are 77.2, 93.2, and 83.0. What explains the changes?

options.text: Increasing depth creates smaller leaves, so the mean is computed from progressively fewer samples
Increasing depth converts salary into a class label
The closest feature value is always returned at every depth
random_state changes the salary units

questions.explanation: A shallow leaf averages many salaries; deeper splits narrow the group. Unlimited depth can effectively memorize a nearby training region.

questions.prompt: To explain one tree prediction, what is the most direct evidence?

options.text: The sequence of feature conditions followed from root to leaf
The average depth of unrelated trees
Every feature in the dataset, whether used or not
The file name of the training data

questions.explanation: A single prediction uses only the features and thresholds on its path. An unused feature does not affect that particular output.

questions.prompt: A candidate has graduation score 21, no IELTS certificate, and minority bonus. The learned path checks score < 19, then IELTS, then score < 24, but never checks the bonus. Why does the bonus not affect this prediction?

options.text: Only conditions on the traversed root-to-leaf path determine the output
Categorical features can never affect decision trees
The bonus is automatically added to the graduation score
All unused features are treated as missing targets

questions.explanation: The sample follows False at score < 19, False for IELTS, and True at score < 24, reaching the not-admitted leaf. The bonus is not on that path.

questions.prompt: Why should built-in impurity-based feature importance be interpreted cautiously?

options.text: It summarizes use in this fitted model, not causality
Correlated features can divide or substitute for one another's importance
Features with many possible split points can receive biased importance
It is guaranteed to equal permutation importance on unseen data

questions.explanation: Impurity importance is convenient but model-specific and can be biased. Validate conclusions with domain knowledge and held-out methods such as permutation importance.

questions.prompt: Two strongly correlated features provide nearly the same signal. What can happen in a fitted tree?

options.text: The tree may select one and make the other appear unimportant even though both are predictive
Both must appear at every node
The tree automatically proves that one causes the target
Correlation prevents any split from being created

questions.explanation: Once one correlated feature captures the gain, the other may add little extra impurity reduction. Importance is therefore not a complete statement about usefulness.

questions.prompt: What probability does a classification-tree leaf commonly report for a class?

options.text: The fraction of training samples in that leaf belonging to the class
The global training accuracy
The number of features used by the tree
A guaranteed perfectly calibrated probability

questions.explanation: Leaf class proportions provide a probability estimate, but small leaves and overfitting can make it poorly calibrated.

questions.prompt: Which practices help when a single decision tree is unstable across small data changes?

options.text: Use cross-validation to measure variability
Regularize the tree with depth or leaf-size constraints
Consider an ensemble such as a random forest or gradient-boosted trees
Judge stability only from training accuracy

questions.explanation: Trees have high variance. Validation reveals it, regularization reduces it, and ensembles average or correct multiple trees to improve stability.

questions.prompt: What does setting random_state mainly provide in a decision-tree experiment?

options.text: Reproducibility for randomized choices or tie behavior used by the implementation
Protection against target leakage
A guarantee of the globally optimal tree
Automatic handling of unseen categories

questions.explanation: A fixed seed helps reproduce a run, but it does not repair weak evaluation, leakage, encoding mistakes, or overfitting.

questions.prompt: Which sequence describes a sound practical decision-tree workflow?

options.text: Define the target, prediction time, and business metric
Split data appropriately, then fit preprocessing and models on training data
Tune complexity on validation data and inspect errors and rules
Use the final test set repeatedly while choosing features
Freeze the pipeline, evaluate once on test data, and monitor after deployment

questions.explanation: The order protects against leakage and test overfitting while keeping model choices tied to the actual decision and operating conditions.

questions.prompt: After deploying a decision tree, what should be monitored?

options.text: Input drift, missing values, and unseen-category rates
Prediction and business performance once labels become available
Performance by important user or risk groups
Whether the production preprocessing contract still matches training
Only whether the service returns HTTP 200

questions.explanation: Service uptime is necessary but not sufficient. Data quality, drift, subgroup behavior, and delayed outcome quality determine whether the model remains useful and safe.
